strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in knowledge-intensive VQA with a coherent, training-free framework combining iterative retrieval, complementary queries, heterogeneous knowledge sources, and accumulated reasoning records.

The within-framework ablations provide promising evidence of practical benefit. In Table 6, adding iteration increases InfoSeek Cover EM from 54.11 to 61.84 and Encyclopedic VQA BEM from 56.67 to 63.33; the latter supports improvements beyond answer-substring matching.

The evaluation explores several benchmarks, model capacities, retrieval budgets, and knowledge-source configurations. The supplied prompts, retrieval-index description, and latency measurements provide useful implementation detail.
weaknesses: The headline retrieval comparisons are not comparable at the stated cutoff. Tables 1–2 place cumulative recall across four iterations and multiple queries under R@5/PRR@5 alongside single-pass baselines. Retrieving fewer than five pairs per query does not make the accumulated candidate set a top-five result. Even the vanilla variant averages recall across iterations. These comparisons cannot establish the claimed retrieval superiority without evaluation at matched total retrieval budgets and consistent candidate-set definitions.

The experiments do not adequately isolate adaptive reasoning from additional computation and evidence. The ablations control retrieval budgets across query strategies within a round, but iteration increases total retrieval and model calls. A matched-budget single-pass baseline and a nonadaptive multi-query baseline using the same models and KBs are needed. Comparisons using Gemini-generated records with smaller answerers also change the effective system capacity relative to earlier methods.

The answer-accuracy evidence has important comparability gaps. Table 4 separates full-validation results from a 5K split, yet the text claims superiority over all prior work across those sections. InfoSeek ablations switch from EM to Cover EM, which can reward responses containing incorrect alternatives alongside the answer. OK-VQA lacks the promised standard VQA-score comparison. These issues require consistent splits, standard metrics, and checks that substring matching reflects correct answers.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the approximately 500-example ablation subsets lack exact identifiers, embedding-model specification, thresholds, and ordering; the Wikipedia-section summarization procedure and Google Lens integration are underspecified; and generation settings and precise API versions are absent. The main text specifies four-shot InfoSeek prompting, whereas Appendix D specifies three demonstrations. Table 4 and Table 5 report different Gemini InfoSeek EM values without clearly explaining the evaluation difference.

The stronger claims about compositional reasoning are not directly demonstrated. Aggregate accuracy and recall do not establish successful composition of visual-to-visual, visual-to-text, and text-to-text links. There is no targeted reasoning analysis or controlled comparison with an adapted iterative text-RAG method to substantiate the claimed need for this specialized design. Small ablation subsets also lack uncertainty estimates.

The contribution is promising, but the unresolved evaluation and reproducibility issues prevent a clear Findings recommendation. Corrected retrieval comparisons, matched-budget controls, and a reconciled evaluation protocol appear feasible within a revision cycle; the concern is evidential soundness rather than simply limited novelty.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in knowledge-intensive VQA with a coherent framework: reasoning records guide query expansion and generation, retrieval combines textual and multimodal knowledge, and accumulated evidence supports the final answer.

The component ablations provide encouraging evidence beyond comparisons with prior systems. In Table 6, combining multi-query retrieval and heterogeneous knowledge sources improves performance on both datasets, with further gains from iteration. Table 8 also supports the usefulness of textual knowledge alongside image–text pairs.

The manuscript provides pseudocode, core prompts, retrieval implementation details, and computational-cost measurements. Evaluation across three benchmarks and multiple model configurations gives useful breadth.
weaknesses: The headline retrieval comparisons are not budget-comparable. Tables 1–2 place cumulative recall across four iterations in R@5/PRR@5 columns alongside conventional fixed-k retrieval results. Retrieving fewer than five pairs per query does not make the union across queries and iterations equivalent to top-5 retrieval. The vanilla variant also averages recall across iterations rather than evaluating a conventional single pass. These results demonstrate eventual evidence coverage, but do not establish the claimed superiority at matched retrieval budgets.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the benefit of the proposed iterative reasoning mechanism. The ablations control retrieval budgets within a round, but iteration increases total retrieved evidence and model computation. A single-pass baseline with a matched total evidence budget, repeated retrieval without reasoning feedback, and a straightforward adaptation of an existing iterative RAG method would help distinguish the proposed contribution from additional inference resources. Describing Google Lens initialization as isolating iterative reasoning is likewise unsupported without a corresponding non-iterative control.

Several accuracy comparisons confound framework improvements with model and evaluation differences. Table 4 explicitly separates full-validation results from a 5K subset, yet the text claims superiority over all prior work across these sections. Results using LLaVA-MORE also consume reasoning records generated by Gemini, so they do not isolate improvements to the original LLaVA-based system. Stronger matched-backbone, matched-split comparisons are needed to substantiate the state-of-the-art claims.

The evaluation protocol weakens confidence in the ablation conclusions. Most analyses use approximately 500 questions selected by a semantic-diversity heuristic, without uncertainty estimates or evidence that the gains generalize to the original distribution. InfoSeek ablations switch from exact match to answer containment, which can reward responses containing multiple or contradictory candidate answers. The large EM–Cover EM differences in Table 5 warrant answer-format controls or a correctness audit. OK-VQA also lacks a clear comparison against prior answer-accuracy results.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix. The subset encoder, similarity thresholds, ordering, and selected IDs are unspecified; corpus versions, Wikipedia-section summarization, generation settings, Google Lens integration, and retrieval allocation/deduplication need clearer documentation. The main text specifies four-shot InfoSeek prompting, whereas Appendix D specifies three demonstrations. Appendix C also labels the same SigLIP2 image-only values as R@1/5/10 that Table 1 labels R@5/10/20, leaving the retrieval protocol ambiguous.

The claims about compositional reasoning and scalability exceed the evidence presented. Aggregate answer accuracy does not establish that the system constructs the proposed cross-modal factual links; targeted reasoning diagnostics or error analysis would strengthen that interpretation. The latency measurements establish appreciable computational costs, while proposed efficiency improvements remain untested. Overall, the approach is promising, but the comparison and reproducibility issues require important revisions before a sound Findings recommendation; they appear addressable within a review cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: combining visual entity grounding with external textual knowledge for knowledge-intensive VQA. The proposed loop of query expansion, follow-up query generation, retrieval, and evidence summarization is coherent and understandable.

The controlled component ablations provide promising evidence. In Table 6, combining multi-query retrieval and heterogeneous knowledge sources improves both benchmarks, and adding iteration increases InfoSeek Cover EM from 54.11 to 61.84 and Encyclopedic VQA BEM from 56.67 to 63.33. Table 8 also supports the usefulness of complementary textual knowledge.

The evaluation explores three benchmarks, multiple model configurations, retrieval budgets, and iteration counts. Prompt templates, retrieval-index details, and a computational-cost analysis provide useful implementation information.
weaknesses: The headline retrieval comparisons are not comparable at the stated cutoff. Tables 1–2 place cumulative recall over multiple queries and four iterations in the R@5/PRR@5 columns alongside baselines retrieving five items. Retrieving fewer than five pairs per query does not make the accumulated result Recall@5. The vanilla variant also averages recall across iterations. These results demonstrate broader evidence coverage, but do not establish superior retrieval at a fixed budget. Report unique-document budgets and compare recall at matched total retrieval budgets.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the claimed advantage of reasoning-guided iteration. The iterative system receives more retrieval and inference opportunities than the single-pass ablations; no matched-total-budget nonadaptive multi-query baseline or direct adaptation of an existing iterative RAG method is evaluated. Headline accuracy comparisons also change model capacity, and several smaller answerers receive Gemini-generated reasoning records. The within-model ablations are valuable, but insufficient to attribute the broader gains specifically to the proposed reasoning mechanism.

Accuracy reporting weakens the state-of-the-art claims. Table 4 separates full-validation results from a 5K subset containing the proposed method, yet the text claims superiority over all prior work. InfoSeek ablations switch from EM to answer-substring Cover EM, which can reward responses containing an answer alongside incorrect alternatives; no human validation establishes that this measures correctness reliably. OK-VQA lacks a main comparative answer-accuracy table using the promised standard VQA score.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The approximately 500-example ablation subsets lack exact sample identifiers, selection thresholds, and the embedding model used for selection. Important details of Wikipedia-section summarization, Google Lens initialization, decoding settings, and query-budget allocation are also unspecified. These omissions affect both the knowledge available to the system and the ability to reproduce its central results.

Several inconsistencies require reconciliation: Section 4.1 specifies four-shot prompting while Appendix D provides three demonstrations; Table 5 reports Gemini InfoSeek EM of 50.8 versus 48.0 in Table 4 without clearly explaining the evaluation difference; and Appendix C appears to relabel the main table's SigLIP2 R@5/R@10/R@20 values as R@1/R@5/R@10. Ablations on small selected subsets also lack uncertainty estimates.

The decisive limitation is evidential, rather than lack of interest or architectural novelty. The reported ablations suggest a potentially publishable contribution, but the unmatched retrieval comparisons, incomplete evaluation controls, and reproduction gaps prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current version. Corrected reporting and targeted controlled experiments could reasonably support a next-cycle resubmission.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: integrating visual grounding with external knowledge retrieval. PMSR is clearly described, with explicit retrieval equations and prompts, and offers a practical approach to iterative multimodal question answering.

The controlled ablations provide meaningful evidence of benefit. On E-VQA, adding iterations to the dual-query, heterogeneous-KB configuration improves BEM from 37.3 to 46.4; removing the record-level query reduces performance to 43.1. These results support the usefulness of the proposed combination independently of comparisons with published systems.

Evaluation spans six benchmarks, multiple model sizes, and both fixed-KB and web-search settings. Adaptive stopping reduces average iterations from five to approximately 3.3–3.5 with modest accuracy losses. The appendices provide useful prompts, retrieval implementation details, sensitivity analyses, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The headline retrieval comparisons do not establish superior retrieval under comparable budgets. Tables 1–2 compare PMSR's cumulative recall across multiple rounds, retrieving up to 30 candidates per round from two KBs, against baselines' R@5/10/20. Higher cumulative coverage is expected with more retrieval opportunities. Appendix G provides per-round results but does not resolve the total-budget mismatch. Matched-budget single-pass and iterative baselines are needed to substantiate the central retrieval claim.

The strongest end-to-end comparisons confound the framework with other changes. Most InfoSeek baselines use the full validation set while PMSR uses the 5K M2KR subset; the strongest E-VQA result uses Gemini against different backbones. Using a common final answerer within PMSR does not control the reasoning models used to construct its input. Web comparisons also involve different search infrastructure, and PMSR additionally uses GPT-OSS-120B for summarization and query rewriting. These results demonstrate competitive systems, but do not cleanly attribute superiority to PMSR.

The claimed reduction in error propagation is insufficiently isolated. There is no direct ablation comparing fresh-evidence record generation with history-conditioned generation under otherwise identical settings. Appendix N compares trajectory categories with WebWatcher using the same KB and retriever, but does not sufficiently specify matched backbone, budgets, or adaptation details. Furthermore, record-level correctness is not equivalent to successful answering: E-VQA's stable-correct plus correction rate is approximately 77.8%, versus 46.4% final BEM. The paper acknowledges this gap, but its analysis does not establish that the proposed mechanism causes more reliable reasoning.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the helpful appendices. Decoding settings, context and record-length limits, evidence ordering and truncation, and web-search top-k and collection dates are not adequately specified. The construction of the single-pass dual-scope ablation also needs clarification, since the defined trajectory-level query requires existing reasoning records. These details materially affect cost, retrieved evidence, and outcomes.

Several claims exceed the precision of the evidence. No uncertainty estimates accompany small web-benchmark differences; the 0.5-point MMSearch improvement corresponds to approximately one question among 171. Efficiency is measured through iteration counts without token, latency, or tool-call costs. Overall, the internal ablations make this a credible candidate for Findings, but unresolved comparison and reproducibility issues prevent a clear positive recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant multimodal NLP problem: acquiring and integrating external evidence for knowledge-intensive VQA. The pipeline is understandable, and generating each reasoning record from fresh evidence provides a plausible mechanism for limiting direct inheritance of earlier mistakes.

The strongest evidence comes from internal ablations. On E-VQA, adding dual-scope queries to the iterative heterogeneous-KB configuration improves BEM from 43.1 to 46.4 with the per-iteration retrieval budget held fixed. Table 5 also shows substantial answer-quality gains over initialization.

Evaluation covers six benchmarks and several model backbones. The appendices provide prompts, retrieval implementation details, knowledge-source ablations, sensitivity analyses, and image-deduplication procedures, making the experimental investigation more substantial than the headline comparisons alone suggest.
Adaptive stopping offers a useful measured tradeoff: average iterations decrease from 5 to 3.3–3.5, with losses of 1.2 CEM points on InfoSeek and 0.7 BEM points on E-VQA.
weaknesses: The headline retrieval comparisons do not establish superior retrieval under comparable budgets. Tables 1–2 compare PMSR's cumulative recall across multiple rounds and heterogeneous sources against baselines' fixed R@5/10/20. Inspecting more candidates naturally increases coverage. Appendix G provides helpful per-round results, but does not replace comparisons controlling the total evidence budget and knowledge sources.

End-to-end comparisons have substantial confounds. Table 3 mixes the full InfoSeek validation set with the M2KR subset, and varies retrievers and reasoning backbones. Fixing the final answerer across PMSR configurations does not isolate the framework from the stronger model producing its reasoning records. On E-VQA, Qwen3-VL-8B PMSR scores 46.4, below OMGM's reported 50.2/51.2; the strongest result uses Gemini without a corresponding same-backbone baseline. The broad claims of consistent superiority therefore exceed the evidence.

Reduced error propagation is not cleanly demonstrated. Table 6 does not directly ablate fresh-evidence record generation against history-conditioned generation with otherwise identical settings. Appendix N controls the KB and retriever for WebWatcher, but leaves other important matching details unspecified. Persistent failure alone does not establish propagation of earlier errors. Moreover, trajectory queries and final answers still consume all previous records.

The trajectory analysis needs a better-validated correctness protocol. Applying CEM/BEM to explanatory records does not necessarily establish correct grounding or reasoning, particularly when records contain multiple candidate facts. On E-VQA, Stable-Correct plus Correction reaches 77.79%, versus 46.4% final-answer BEM. The paper acknowledges this gap, but the oracle-context experiment does not directly validate record scoring or explain the discrepancy.

Several evaluation and reproducibility details remain unresolved: decoding settings, context truncation and record-length limits, web top-k values, search dates or cached outputs, and the precise WebWatcher adaptation. The web variant additionally uses GPT-OSS-120B for summarization and rewriting, complicating the same-backbone comparison. Small gains such as 54.3 versus 53.8 on the 171-question MMSearch subset are presented without uncertainty estimates.

The stopping criterion takes the maximum similarity over query pairs, so one repeated query can terminate retrieval even when the other query introduces new information. Its saturation interpretation needs validation against alternative stopping rules and thresholds. Overall, the internal ablations support a promising, potentially Findings-worthy contribution, but unresolved comparison and measurement issues prevent a clear positive recommendation; these concerns concern evidential adequacy rather than lack of novelty alone.

strengths: PMSR addresses a relevant multimodal NLP problem with a clear, implementable framework: complementary record-level and trajectory-level queries retrieve heterogeneous evidence, which is summarized into records for subsequent reasoning.

The controlled ablations provide credible evidence of practical benefit. On E-VQA, the full method achieves 46.4 BEM versus 43.1 without dual-scope queries and 37.3 without iteration (Table 6). Fixed-iteration results also show substantial answer-quality gains beyond initialization (Table 5).
Evaluation spans six benchmarks, multiple model backbones, and both Wikipedia and web retrieval. The appendices add useful retriever, retrieval-budget, context-noise, and query-weight analyses.

Adaptive termination offers a concrete efficiency tradeoff: average iterations decrease from five to 3.3–3.5, with relatively small accuracy reductions (Table 7). The paper also acknowledges inference overhead and reports local latency.

Equations, operator prompts, retrieval implementation, dataset descriptions, and evaluation prompts make the core method reasonably reproducible. Overall, the controlled results support a useful contribution suitable for Findings, even though the broader superiority and mechanism claims need qualification.
weaknesses: The headline retrieval comparisons are not budget matched. Tables 1–2 compare PMSR's cumulative recall across multiple rounds and heterogeneous sources with baselines' fixed R@k or PRR@k. Greater evidence exposure can itself increase recall. Appendix G provides per-round results but does not establish superiority under equal total retrieval budgets and knowledge access.

End-to-end comparisons only partially isolate the framework's contribution. Most InfoSeek baselines use the full validation set, whereas PMSR uses the 5K M2KR subset; models and retrievers also differ. Holding the final InfoSeek answerer fixed across PMSR configurations does not control differences in trajectory-generation models or establish a matched comparison with prior systems. The web variant additionally uses GPT-OSS-120B for summarization and query rewriting, complicating the same-backbone framing.

The central explanation that independent compact records reduce error propagation is less firmly established than the accuracy gains. There is no direct ablation comparing fresh-evidence record generation with history-conditioned record generation under otherwise identical conditions. Appendix N controls the KB and retriever for WebWatcher, but gives insufficient detail about other controls and how intermediate correctness is made comparable. Scoring long records with CEM/BEM also does not directly validate grounding or factual consistency.

Several evaluation claims require more caution. Small web-benchmark gains lack uncertainty estimates, particularly on the 171-question MMSearch subset. OK-VQA uses an LLM judge rather than its conventional accuracy metric. The conclusion's claim of consistent improvement over strong baselines overstates the mixed results: PMSR trails DeepEyesV2 on MMSearch, and its Qwen3-VL-8B configuration trails OMGM on E-VQA.

Reproducibility is stronger for the core algorithm than for exact experimental results. Decoding settings, precise API model versions, web-search dates or cached responses, and some web retrieval budgets are unspecified. The stopping rule also uses the maximum similarity across any query pair, so one repeated query can stop the process despite novelty in the other branch; threshold sensitivity and a comparison with a cheaper fixed three- or four-iteration policy would better justify this choice.
